clue.text: The goal of the extremist ?

parts.note: an extremist aims to go as far as possible, so the goal is the furthest point one can reach

explanation.surface: A question about what fanatics are ultimately aiming for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goal' suggests a political aim, but read literally the extremist goes to the extreme, the outermost bound.
explanation.definitionFit: The extreme point beyond which nothing goes is the boundary or utmost extent.

clue.text: Formby's street-corner supporters

parts.note: George Formby, the British comic singer, sang Leaning on a Lamp-post, about standing on a street corner

explanation.surface: Fans of an entertainer gathered on a street corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' suggests fans; it means things he leaned on. George Formby was a British ukulele-playing comedian famous for that song.
explanation.definitionFit: The street lights on corners physically held up the singer leaning against them in the song.

clue.text: Met to' compose choral work

indicators.note: compose means put together in a new arrangement, so the letters of met and to are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to a composer, met with, to write a piece for choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compose' fits the musical surface, but it is the anagram signal working on METTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A short sacred piece for unaccompanied voices is a classic choral form.

clue.text: A number of workers in occupation

definitions.note: a phrase for those in occupation, defining the plural noun

parts.note: ten is a number
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: A count of employees in some trade or profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupation' suggests a job for the workers; it means occupying property, as those who rent do.
explanation.definitionFit: Renters living in a property are its occupiers.

clue.text: It's very off-putting

parts.note: off-putting read literally as putting things off, postponing them

explanation.surface: Something described as thoroughly unpleasant or repellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-putting' normally means unpleasant; here it means putting off till later, so the answer is a postponement.
explanation.definitionFit: A postponement or delay is literally the act of putting something off.

clue.text: "We are such stuff As — are made on" (Tempest)

definitions.text: "We are such stuff As — are made on" (Tempest)

parts.words: "We are such stuff As — are made on" (Tempest)
parts.note: Prospero's speech in Shakespeare's The Tempest, completed by the missing word

explanation.surface: A famous line from Shakespeare with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Prospero's line: 'We are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep'.
explanation.definitionFit: The visions of sleep are the missing word in the quoted line.

clue.text: Do they pass quickly in Ramadan ?

definitions.text: Do they pass quickly in Ramadan ?

parts.words: Do they pass quickly in Ramadan
parts.note: fast as speedy, or fast as going without food, which Muslims do in the holy month

explanation.surface: Asking whether time flies during the Muslim holy month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass quickly' leads to the speedy sense of 'fast'; Ramadan points to the religious sense, abstaining from food.
explanation.definitionFit: Days of abstaining from food, as in the Muslim holy month, could be read as speedy days.

clue.text: Old party getting: at the root of things

explanation.surface: An old political party getting down to fundamentals.
explanation.walkthrough: The Radicals were a nineteenth-century British political grouping; the word also comes from Latin radix, root.
explanation.definitionFit: The Radicals were a historic British political faction, and the word also means fundamental, going to the root.

clue.text: Mission youth delivers the goods

definitions.note: describes one who delivers the goods, defining the noun

parts.note: an errand is a small mission or task
a boy is a youth

explanation.surface: A young man on a special assignment who brings in results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivers the goods' is an idiom for succeeding, but here it is literal: a lad who carries shopping to customers.
explanation.definitionFit: A lad employed to run messages and carry purchases to customers literally brings the goods round.

clue.text: Features of those who are long in the tooth?

definitions.text: Features of those who are long in the tooth?

parts.words: Features of those who are long in the tooth
parts.note: long in the tooth means old, but literally describes animals with very long teeth such as elephants

explanation.surface: A question about the characteristics of elderly people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long in the tooth' means elderly; taken literally it points to elephants, walruses and boars with protruding teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Elongated protruding teeth of elephants and walruses are literally long teeth.

clue.text: They weren't entitled 'to the King's Bounty

definitions.text: They weren't entitled 'to the King's Bounty

parts.words: They weren't entitled 'to the King's Bounty
parts.note: the Bounty was the Royal Navy ship (His Majesty's Armed Vessel) whose crew rose against Captain Bligh in 1789 and seized it

explanation.surface: Some people were denied a share of the royal generosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounty' looks like a handout from the King; it is HMAV Bounty, the King's ship, which its crew had no right to take.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors who seized the ship from its captain in revolt had no lawful claim to it.

clue.text: Makes repairs to a ladder, perhaps.

definitions.text: Makes repairs to a ladder, perhaps.

parts.words: Makes repairs to a ladder, perhaps
parts.note: a ladder is also a run in a stocking, which is mended with needle and thread

explanation.surface: Someone fixing a broken rung on their stepladder.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'ladder' in British English is a run in tights or stockings, mended by sewing rather than carpentry.
explanation.definitionFit: Mending a hole or run in fabric by weaving thread across it is the needlework sense.

clue.text: Obvious remedies ?

parts.note: patent can mean obvious, and remedies are medicines, so the phrase names proprietary over-the-counter cures

explanation.surface: A question about cures that are plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obvious' is one sense of 'patent'; the other sense is a protected trade name, as on branded proprietary cures.
explanation.definitionFit: Proprietary cures sold under a registered trade name are the protected, branded sort of remedy.

clue.text: Life member of a union

parts.note: the union is a marriage, and each partner joins it for life

explanation.surface: A trade unionist who holds lifelong membership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union; it is the union of marriage, whose members are partners for life.
explanation.definitionFit: A husband or wife is a partner in a marriage, joined until death.

clue.text: One place your parents can't get you into.

definitions.text: One place your parents can't get you into.

parts.words: One place your parents can't get you into
parts.note: only a child without living parents is admitted, so the parents cannot be the ones to place them there

explanation.surface: A club or school that family influence cannot open up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an exclusive school; the place is a home for children whose parents have died.
explanation.definitionFit: A home for parentless children admits only those whose mother and father are gone.

clue.text: Of course, it's just a summary

definitions.text: Of course, it's just a summary

parts.words: Of course, it's just a summary
parts.note: an outline listing the topics of a course of study

explanation.surface: Someone shrugging that a document is merely a brief overview.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as 'naturally'; here it means 'belonging to a course of study'.
explanation.definitionFit: The outline of subjects for a course of study is a summary of what it covers.

clue.text: Madly sent gross, of birds

indicators.note: madly says the letters of the next words are thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone wildly dispatching a hundred and forty-four birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' looks like a dozen dozen; it is just fodder, and 'Madly' rearranges SENTGROSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Songbirds are poetically called singers.

clue.text: Mice and men for instance

parts.note: Burns's poem To a Mouse says the best-laid plans of mice and men often go wrong

explanation.surface: Examples of creatures, rodents and humans alike.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns wrote 'The best laid schemes o' mice an' men gang aft agley', so mice and men are plotters.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who lay plans or plots are, in Burns's line, mice and men.

clue.text: What comes of growing sage ?

parts.note: sage as an adjective means wise, so growing sage is becoming wise

explanation.surface: A gardener wondering what results from cultivating the herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sage' is the herb in the surface; the clue means becoming sage, wise, and the result is wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisdom or discernment is what one acquires by becoming wise.

clue.text: Exercised right to spread grass 'below' the river

indicators.note: below places the following pieces after the river in this down entry

parts.note: the Exe is the river in Devon, a crossword regular
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry as hay

explanation.surface: Someone had the right to scatter cut grass beneath the river bank.
explanation.walkthrough: TED is a farming word for spreading mown grass to dry; the Exe is a river in Devon, England.
explanation.definitionFit: To have exercised influence or effort is to have applied or used it.

clue.text: It included Clementine's father's cavern

parts.note: in the song Oh My Darling, Clementine, her father, a miner, lived in a cavern in a deep gorge

explanation.surface: A place that once contained the home of a girl's dad.
explanation.walkthrough: The American folk song begins 'In a cavern, in a canyon, excavating for a mine, dwelt a miner, forty-niner, and his daughter Clementine'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep steep-sided gorge is the place that held the miner's cavern in the song.

clue.text: Shaped, like a needle or a donkey, 'say ?

explanation.surface: Something pointed like a needle, or perhaps shaped like a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is from Latin acus, needle; 'say' signals that the word also sounds like 'ass-iform', donkey-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: The botanical term for needle-shaped, which also sounds as if built from ass, a donkey.

clue.text: Some comedians, use them if they, are wise

definitions.text: Some comedians, use them if they, are wise

parts.words: Some comedians, use them if they, are wise
parts.note: jokes are used by comedians, and adding wise in front makes a word for smart remarks

explanation.surface: Sensible comedians would make use of certain things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If they are wise' reads as prudent; it means the jokes are wise ones, wisecracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Quips or jokes, especially smart ones, are what comedians tell.

clue.text: Their act goes with a swing

definitions.text: Their act goes with a swing

parts.words: Their act goes with a swing
parts.note: goes with a swing means goes well, but here the performers literally use a swinging bar

explanation.surface: Praise for performers whose show is lively and successful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes with a swing' is an idiom for a lively success; these circus performers literally work on a swinging bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Circus acrobats performing on a high swinging bar do their act on a swing.

clue.text: Banned, thanks to obvious disapproval.

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks
boo is a loud jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: Something prohibited because of plain public objection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thanks to' looks like 'because of', but 'thanks' gives TA, British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forbidden by custom or social rule is prohibited.

clue.text: A reproach that takes on in Somerset"

definitions.text: A reproach that takes on in Somerset"

parts.words: A reproach that takes on in Somerset
parts.note: a word for a jeer that, taking on the letters ON, becomes the county town of Somerset

explanation.surface: A rebuke that catches on in a West Country county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes on' suggests catching on; literally the word takes ON to become Taunton, the county town of Somerset in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeer or insulting remark is a kind of reproach.

clue.text: Surprising for him to, be a little saint

definitions.text: Surprising for him to, be a little saint

parts.note: taken as written
ST is the short form of saint

explanation.surface: Someone remarking that a rough fellow behaving angelically would be a surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a brute, for whom saintliness would be surprising; the last words also spell the answer as BE A ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A brutish or savage person would hardly be expected to act angelically.

clue.text: It's enveloped with railings perhaps

explanation.surface: Something wrapped up inside, perhaps fenced in.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is an item put in an envelope with a letter; the other is a fenced-off area, as at a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sent inside a letter's envelope, and also a fenced or walled-off piece of ground.

clue.text: In the case of 11, they're too much of a good thing.

definitions.text: In the case of 11, they're too much of a good thing.

parts.words: In the case of 11, they're too much of a good thing
parts.note: taking too much of a medicine is harmful, an excess of something beneficial

explanation.surface: A comment that even welcome things can be overdone.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to 11 across, branded cures; too large a quantity of a medicine is an excess of a good thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive quantities of a drug taken at once are an excess of something beneficial.

clue.text: Times' change' for tiny ones

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: A remark that the era moves on, for the small folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times change' reads as a proverb, but 'change' is the anagram signal working on TIMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Very small creatures such as tiny arachnids, or small children, are called by this word.
